title: The printed thermal diversity index in a Finnish five-group study can fall when thermal spread rises
abstract: We audited the thermal diversity equation in a 2025 Finnish study of five groups. Its stated index equals the abundance-weighted population standard deviation divided by the square root of species richness minus one. An exact example has a 20 percent increase in thermal spread but a 31 percent decrease in the index. We then fitted within-site log-index trends to public Finnish summaries. Conditional on the printed equation, annual log increases in richness minus one of 0.84 percent for moths, 0.27 percent for birds and 0.65 percent for plants would remove their negative point trends in thermal spread. These are sensitivity thresholds, not observed richness trends. The release has no richness column or species records, so it cannot establish a corrected trend or confirm the source implementation. The result limits the use of this diversity metric to infer cold-tail loss as a cause of weak thermal tracking. It does not change mean temperature indices or refute separate abundance evidence. We supply a proof, numerical checks, all aggregate fits, source hashes, a figure and an external-data reproduction method.

display.caption: An exact reversal of spread and index, and conditional richness-change thresholds in five Finnish groups. These thresholds do not measure richness change.

citations.reason: The printed thermal diversity equation includes a richness divisor, so its decline does not by itself show a decline in thermal spread.
Public site-year indices give conditional sensitivity thresholds; no source records are bundled.
Weak tracking across networks motivates independent evidence on ecological processes.
Finite summary lag fits leave the ecological mechanism uncertain.
